title: Parts of speech, clauses and phrases
blurb: Name the job of any word in a sentence, and tell a clause (subject + verb) from a phrase (no subject-verb pair).
question: In “Since the clinic moved, parking has been easier,” the word “since” starts a clause. In “Since Monday, parking has been easier,” it starts a phrase. What is the difference, and why does the TEAS care?

teach.h: Words have jobs; word groups have shapes
teach.body: Formally, a part of speech is the grammatical role a word plays in its sentence; a clause is a group of words with a subject and a verb; a phrase is a group of words without a subject-verb pair. Plain English: the same word can change jobs (“since” can be a conjunction or a preposition), so judge each word by what it does in THIS sentence. Then ask of any word group: does it have its own subject and verb? If yes, it is a clause.

head: Part
Job
Examples
rows: Names a person, place, thing, idea
Describes a verb, adjective or adverb
Links a noun to the rest
teach.caption: Articles (a, an, the) work like adjectives. Use “a” before a consonant SOUND (a uniform) and “an” before a vowel SOUND (an hour, an MRI).
Feel, look and taste can be action or linking verbs: “She felt the lump” (action) vs “She felt dizzy” (linking).
Independent clause: stands alone. Dependent clause: starts with a subordinating conjunction or relative pronoun.

root.label: Does it have its own subject and verb?

children.label: Starts with because, when, who, that...

head: Phrase
Built from
Example
rows: Verb form used as an adjective
teach.caption: Gerund vs participle: both can end in -ing, but a gerund acts as a noun and a participle describes a noun.

teach.body: Aaliyah James, a nursing applicant, compares two sentences. “Since the clinic moved, parking has been easier”: after “since” come a subject (the clinic) and a verb (moved), so “since” is a subordinating conjunction starting a dependent clause, making the sentence complex. “Since Monday, parking has been easier”: “Monday” has no verb, so “since” is a preposition starting a phrase, and the sentence is simple.

teach.text: TEAS traps: treating words such as after, before, since and until as conjunctions every time (they are prepositions when no subject and verb follow), calling a gerund a verb, missing a relative pronoun (who, which, that) that starts a dependent clause, and choosing “a” before a silent h or a letter that sounds like a vowel (an hour, an MRI).

items: Judge each word's part of speech by its job in the sentence.
Adverbs modify verbs, adjectives and other adverbs (very calm, works quickly).
Linking verbs connect a subject to a description (seems, feels, is).
A clause has a subject and verb; a phrase does not.
Dependent clauses start with subordinating conjunctions or relative pronouns.

summary: You can now identify the eight parts of speech by their job, tell action, linking and helping verbs apart, and distinguish independent clauses, dependent clauses and phrases. You can also choose a or an by sound and spot when a word like “since” switches jobs.

A.q: In the sentence “She seemed very calm after the long procedure,” what part of speech is “very”?
A.why: “Very” modifies the adjective “calm,” and words that modify adjectives are adverbs.

whyNot.0: Adjectives modify nouns; “very” modifies another describing word, calm.
whyNot.1: A preposition links a noun to the rest of the sentence; “very” has no noun object.
whyNot.3: A pronoun replaces a noun; “very” replaces nothing.

A.q: Which word group is a dependent clause?
options: after the very long night shift
A.why: It has a subject (shift) and verb (ran) and begins with the subordinating conjunction “although.”

whyNot.1: “Running late for the shift” has no subject and no main verb; it is a verbal (-ing) phrase.
whyNot.2: “After the very long night shift” has no verb; “after” is a preposition here.
whyNot.3: This clause has no subordinating word, so it is independent, not dependent.

A.q: In the sentence “Swimming is good exercise for patients,” what is the function of “Swimming”?
A.why: “Swimming” is the subject of “is,” so it is an -ing verb form acting as a noun: a gerund.

whyNot.0: A participle describes a noun; here “swimming” is the subject itself.
whyNot.2: The main verb of the sentence is “is.”

B.q: Which sentence uses the articles a and an correctly?
options: The aide waited a hour for an MRI and a one-time pass.
The aide waited an hour for an MRI and a one-time pass.
The aide waited an hour for a MRI and a one-time pass.
The aide waited an hour for an MRI and an one-time pass.
B.why: Hour and MRI begin with vowel sounds (“ow,” “em”), so they take an; one-time begins with a “w” sound, so it takes a.

whyNot.0: The h in hour is silent, so it starts with a vowel sound: an hour.
whyNot.2: MRI is read “em-ar-eye,” starting with a vowel sound: an MRI.
whyNot.3: One-time is pronounced “won,” starting with a consonant sound: a one-time.

B.q: Which word group is a phrase rather than a clause?
B.why: “After the morning rounds” has no verb: it is a prepositional phrase.

whyNot.0: It has a subject (doctor) and verb (arrives): a dependent clause.
whyNot.1: It has a subject (she) and verb (was): a dependent clause.
whyNot.2: “Who” is the subject and “works” is the verb: a dependent clause.

B.q: In the sentence “The nurse who works nights is my aunt,” what are the words “who works nights”?
B.why: It has a subject (who) and verb (works) and starts with a relative pronoun, so it is a dependent clause.

whyNot.0: “Who works nights” cannot stand alone as a sentence.
whyNot.1: It contains no preposition, and it has a subject-verb pair.
whyNot.3: An appositive is a noun phrase that renames a noun; this has a verb.

C.q: In which sentence is “since” a subordinating conjunction?
options: Since the clinic moved, parking has been easier.
Since Monday, parking has been much easier.
Parking has been easier since last spring.
Since the move in early May, parking has been easier.
C.why: Here “since” is followed by a subject (the clinic) and verb (moved), so it starts a dependent clause.

whyNot.1: “Since Monday” has no verb, so “since” is a preposition.
whyNot.2: “Since last spring” has no verb, so “since” is a preposition.
whyNot.3: “The move” is a noun, not a subject-verb pair, so “since” is a preposition.

C.q: In the sentence “Dr. Lee, the surgeon on call, arrived early,” what are the words “the surgeon on call”?
C.why: The noun phrase renames Dr. Lee and has no verb, so it is an appositive phrase.

whyNot.0: It has no verb, so it is not a clause of any kind.
whyNot.2: It has no verb and cannot stand alone.
whyNot.3: An infinitive phrase begins with “to” + verb.

C.q: Which word in this sentence is a coordinating conjunction? “Although the patient was tired, she walked to the window, for she wanted fresh air.”
C.why: “For” (meaning because) joins two independent clauses after a comma, so it is a coordinating conjunction from FANBOYS.

whyNot.0: “Although” is a subordinating conjunction: it makes its clause dependent.
whyNot.1: “To” is a preposition here, linking “window” to the verb “walked.”
whyNot.2: “She” is a pronoun, the subject of “walked.”

reteach.title: Words are workers with job titles
reteach.question: Think of a sentence as a small team. Each word has a job today, and the same person can do a different job tomorrow. How do you tell who is doing what?

blocks.body: You cannot tell a worker's job from their name, only from what they are doing. “Since” working in front of a full clause (since the clinic moved) is a conjunction; working in front of a single noun (since Monday) it is a preposition. A word group is a full crew (a clause) only if it has both a subject and a verb on shift. Without both, it is a helper crew: a phrase.

blocks.text: Always check what follows: a subject and verb means a clause; a noun alone means a phrase.

explain.body: An action verb shows something done. A linking verb (is, seem, feel, become) connects the subject to a word that describes it. A helping verb (has, will, can) supports a main verb.

test.q: In the sentence “The patient felt dizzy after standing,” what kind of verb is “felt”?
test.why: “Felt” connects the subject (patient) to a describing word (dizzy), so it is a linking verb.

whyNot.0: The patient is not doing something to an object; “felt” links to a description.
whyNot.1: A helping verb supports another verb; here “felt” is the only verb.

explain.body: Choose by sound, not spelling. Use “a” before consonant sounds (a uniform, a one-time fee) and “an” before vowel sounds (an hour, an honest answer, an MRI).

test.q: Which phrase uses the correct article?
test.why: The h in honest is silent, so the word begins with a vowel sound: an honest answer.

whyNot.1: The h in hour is silent, so it needs an: an hour-long wait.
whyNot.2: Uniform begins with a “you” sound (a consonant sound): a uniform.
whyNot.3: MRI begins with the vowel sound “em”: an MRI scan.

explain.body: A dependent clause has a subject and verb but begins with a subordinating conjunction (because, although, when, if, since, until) or a relative pronoun (who, whom, whose, which, that).

test.q: Which word begins the dependent clause in “The chart that you need is on the desk”?
test.why: “That” is a relative pronoun beginning the dependent clause “that you need.”

whyNot.0: “Chart” is the noun the clause describes, not the start of the clause.
whyNot.2: “Need” is the verb inside the dependent clause.
whyNot.3: “On” begins the prepositional phrase “on the desk.”

explain.body: A phrase has no subject-verb pair. Prepositional phrases start with a preposition; infinitive phrases start with “to” + verb; gerund phrases use -ing forms and participial phrases use -ing or past-participle forms; appositives rename a noun.

test.q: Which word group is an infinitive phrase?
test.why: An infinitive phrase begins with “to” plus the base form of a verb: to rest.

whyNot.1: “Resting” is an -ing form, so this is a gerund or participial phrase.
whyNot.2: “Rested” is a past-tense or past-participle form, not “to” + verb.
whyNot.3: This begins with the preposition “after,” so it is a prepositional phrase.
